2052: The respondents were employed in banks which were not governed by the Sastry award as modified by the Labour Appellate Tribunal. 5266: The appellants were the owner of a plot of land in Calcutta. [ 125B C] (iii) The mere fact that the donor has made a will not make the gift does not necessarily lead to the inference that the gift has been made by transfer. The fact that there is a will not affect the validity of

6881: The appellant, a Hindu Undivided Family, was carrying on business in the agricultural lands and village immovable property. In respect of agricultural land and village immovable properties, he purchased the same from the father 's brother or brothers 's son. The vendor 's brother 's son 's son received the same as rent. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1 The right of preemption conferred on the Kinsfolks 'a 'or ' sons 's son or daughters ' sons ' sons ' is a statutory right which can be enforced against the tenant. [314C D] 3.3 The right of an pre emption is a statutory provision and it is open to the legislature to provide that the right should be exercised with due regard to the rights of the preemption. 6668: The appellant and the respondents were brothers. They had a will in respect of certain properties which included the property of the second respondent. 415: The appellant was detained under section 3(2) of the , on 8th June, 1955. He filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging his detention and the order of detention passed by the Government of Bombay dated August 8, 1955. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the grounds furnished in the petition were not relevant to the order of the detention. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the order of detenue was made without any real application of mind by the detaining authority; (ii) the order was vitiated because the detenu had failed to furnish particulars of the grounds which he had stated in the affidavit filed in reply to para 15(g) of the affidavit; (iii) the order did not amount to any prejudicial activity within the meaning of article 19(5)(f) of the Constitution as the detention could not be said to have been for an ulterior motive or purpose. HELD: (1) The order of detention is bad in law and must be set aside. [384 C] (a) It is well settled that the power of detention cannot be exercised against the person who has been deprived of his right to move the court for questioning the validity of the order. If the appellant had exercised his right to ask for particulars, at the time of making the order the court would have gone into the question whether the grounds furnished were good or not. [385 D E] (b) The order was not vitiated by any materiality or ground on the basis of which it could be said that the order was based on some consideration of the representation made by the detenu. The fact that the detenu had not given the grounds does not make the order of Detention. [386 H] (c) The order must be set out in the grounds of detention. The order must also contain a recital that the grounds are sufficient to enable the detenu to meet the existence of facts and circumstances of each case. [397 G H] (d) The order is not vitiated by non communication of the decision. [398 A B] (c). The order must therefore be set aside and the order must be restored. [399 F G]
2248: The appellant was the elected Chairman of a Panchayat. 5142: The petitioner/petitioner was detained under section 3(2) of the , on the ground that he had activities prejudicial to the maintenance of public order. 2065: The appellants, who were the trustees of a temple, filed a suit for possession of certain properties in inam. 1762: The respondent was a resident of the former Dholpur State and the dispute which led to the suit related to a time before the merger of the former Dolpur State into the Matsya Union.
